B.5.2 Reverse KL need not lower bound teacher-weighted likelihood of success

In Proposition 5, we derived that DistIL objective is a lower bound on the teacher-weighted likelihood of success and therefore achieves better Pass@N. Next, we show that this need not hold true for SDPO. Proposition 7 formalizes this distinction by providing a counterexample in which the reverse-KL objective fails to provide such a lower bound. The construction considers a two-action setting in which the teacher assigns twice as much probability mass (2​δ2\delta) to the correct response as the student (δ\delta). As the teacher and student success probabilities simultaneously approach zero, the reverse-KL divergence scales as O⁡(δ)O(\delta), whereas the magnitude of the teacher-weighted log-likelihood term, |pπT​(x)​log⁡pπθ​(x)|\bigl|p_{\pi_{T}}(x)\log p_{\pi_{\theta}}(x)\bigr|, scales as Θ⁡(δ​log⁡(1/δ))\Theta\bigl(\delta\log(1/\delta)\bigr). Since δ​log⁡(1/δ)\delta\log(1/\delta) dominates δ\delta as δ→0\delta\to 0, the reverse-KL term becomes asymptotically negligible relative to the teacher-weighted log-likelihood term. Consequently, the reverse-KL objective need not provide a lower bound on the teacher-weighted log-likelihood of success.

Proposition 7 (Reverse KL need not lower bound teacher-weighted likelihood of success).

There exists a prompt xx, a teacher policy πT\pi_{T}, and a student policy πθ\pi_{\theta} with pπT​(x)>pπθ​(x)p_{\pi_{T}}(x)>p_{\pi_{\theta}}(x), i.e., the teacher is strictly better than the student, such that

−DKL(πθ(⋅∣x)∥πT(⋅∣x))>pπT(x)logpπθ(x),-D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\big(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid x)\big)\;>\;p_{\pi_{T}}(x)\log p_{\pi_{\theta}}(x),

and hence minimizing the reverse KL does not maximize a lower bound on the teacher-weighted log-likelihood of success.

Now, we provide a detailed analysis of Proposition 7. Consider a two-response setting 𝒴={y+,y−}\mathcal{Y}=\{y^{+},y^{-}\} with r⁡(x,y+)=1r(x,y^{+})=1 and r⁡(x,y−)=0r(x,y^{-})=0. For δ∈(0,12)\delta\in\left(0,\tfrac{1}{2}\right), set

πT​(y+∣x)=2​δ,πθ​(y+∣x)=δ,\pi_{T}(y^{+}\mid x)=2\delta,\qquad\pi_{\theta}(y^{+}\mid x)=\delta,

so that pπT​(x)=2​δ>δ=pπθ​(x)p_{\pi_{T}}(x)=2\delta>\delta=p_{\pi_{\theta}}(x). The reverse KL divergence evaluates to

DKL(πθ∥πT)=δlogδ2​δ+(1−δ)log1−δ1−2​δ=−δlog2+(1−δ)log1−δ1−2​δ≈δ(1−log2)as δ→0,D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{T})=\delta\log\frac{\delta}{2\delta}+(1-\delta)\log\frac{1-\delta}{1-2\delta}=-\delta\log 2+(1-\delta)\log\frac{1-\delta}{1-2\delta}\;\approx\;\delta(1-\log 2)\quad\text{as }\delta\to 0,

where we used the Taylor expansion (1−δ)​log⁡1−δ1−2​δ≈δ(1-\delta)\log\frac{1-\delta}{1-2\delta}\approx\delta as δ→0\delta\to 0. Meanwhile, the teacher-weighted log-likelihood of success satisfies

pπT​(x)​log⁡pπθ​(x)=2​δ​log⁡δ,p_{\pi_{T}}(x)\log p_{\pi_{\theta}}(x)=2\delta\log\delta,

so −pπT​(x)​log⁡pπθ​(x)=−2​δ​log⁡δ-p_{\pi_{T}}(x)\log p_{\pi_{\theta}}(x)=-2\delta\log\delta. Since −2​δ​log⁡δ≫δ⁡(1−log⁡2)-2\delta\log\delta\gg\delta(1-\log 2) as δ→0\delta\to 0, we conclude that for all sufficiently small δ>0\delta>0,

DKL(πθ(⋅∣x)∥πT(⋅∣x))<−pπT(x)logpπθ(x),D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\big(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid x)\big)\;<\;-p_{\pi_{T}}(x)\log p_{\pi_{\theta}}(x),

which is equivalent to

−DKL(πθ(⋅∣x)∥πT(⋅∣x))>pπT(x)logpπθ(x).-D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\big(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_{T}(\cdot\mid x)\big)\;>\;p_{\pi_{T}}(x)\log p_{\pi_{\theta}}(x).

Thus, unlike the forward cross-entropy of DistIL, the negative reverse KL cannot serve as a lower bound on the teacher-weighted log-likelihood of success, even when the teacher is strictly better than the student.

B.6 Technical Lemmas

Lemma 1 (Fisher identity for softmax policies).

Let πθ\pi_{\theta} be a softmax policy over a finite action set 𝒜\mathcal{A}, with

πθ​(a)=eθa∑b∈𝒜eθb.\pi_{\theta}(a)=\frac{e^{\theta_{a}}}{\sum_{b\in\mathcal{A}}e^{\theta_{b}}}.

Define the score vector sa:=∇θ​log​πθ​(a)s_{a}:=\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(a), and the Fisher information matrix F⁡(θ)=𝔼a∼πθ​[sa​sa⊤]F(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim\pi_{\theta}}\!\left[s_{a}s_{a}^{\top}\right]. Then, for any a,b∈𝒜a,b\in\mathcal{A},

sa⊤​F​(θ)−1​sb=𝟏{a=b}πθ​(b)−1.s_{a}^{\top}F(\theta)^{-1}s_{b}=\frac{\mathbf{1}\{a=b\}}{\pi_{\theta}(b)}-1.

Equivalently, πθ(a)sa⊤F(θ)−1sb=𝟏{a=b}−πθ(a)\pi_{\theta}(a)\,s_{a}^{\top}F(\theta)^{-1}s_{b}=\mathbf{1}\{a=b\}-\pi_{\theta}(a).

Proof.

Let m:=|𝒜|m:=|\mathcal{A}| and we write pa:=πθ​(a)p_{a}:=\pi_{\theta}(a). Let ea∈ℝme_{a}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} denote the aa-th standard basis vector, and let 𝟏∈ℝm\mathbf{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} denote the all-ones vector. Then, for the softmax parameterization, we have

∂log⁡πθ​(a)∂θc=𝟏{a=c}−pc.\frac{\partial\log\pi_{\theta}(a)}{\partial\theta_{c}}=\mathbf{1}\{a=c\}-p_{c}.

Hence, sa=ea−ps_{a}=e_{a}-p, where p=(p1,…,pm)⊤p=(p_{1},\dots,p_{m})^{\top}.

Now, by definition, F⁡(θ)=𝔼a∼p​[(ea−p)​(ea−p)⊤]F(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim p}\!\left[(e_{a}-p)(e_{a}-p)^{\top}\right]. Upon expanding, we get F⁡(θ)=𝔼a∼p​[ea​ea⊤]−p​p⊤F(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{a\sim p}[e_{a}e_{a}^{\top}]-pp^{\top}. Since 𝔼a∼p​[ea​ea⊤]=diag⁡(p)\mathbb{E}_{a\sim p}[e_{a}e_{a}^{\top}]=\mathrm{diag}(p), we obtain

F⁡(θ)=diag⁡(p)−p​p⊤.F(\theta)=\mathrm{diag}(p)-pp^{\top}.

Next, we fix b∈𝒜b\in\mathcal{A}, and define v:=ebpb−𝟏v:=\frac{e_{b}}{p_{b}}-\mathbf{1}. We claim that F⁡(θ)​v=sbF(\theta)v=s_{b}. For this, we note that p⊤​v=∑a∈𝒜pa​(𝟏{a=b}pb−1)=1−1=0p^{\top}v=\sum_{a\in\mathcal{A}}p_{a}\left(\frac{\mathbf{1}\{a=b\}}{p_{b}}-1\right)=1-1=0. Therefore,

F⁡(θ)​v=(diag⁡(p)−p​p⊤)​v=diag⁡(p)​v−p⁡(p⊤​v)=diag⁡(p)​v.F(\theta)v=(\mathrm{diag}(p)-pp^{\top})v=\mathrm{diag}(p)v-p(p^{\top}v)=\mathrm{diag}(p)v.

Now,

diag⁡(p)​v=diag⁡(p)​(ebpb−𝟏)=eb−p=sb.\mathrm{diag}(p)v=\mathrm{diag}(p)\left(\frac{e_{b}}{p_{b}}-\mathbf{1}\right)=e_{b}-p=s_{b}.

Thus, F⁡(θ)​v=sbF(\theta)v=s_{b}. Now, assuming that inverse of F⁡(θ)F(\theta) exists, we have

F​(θ)−1​sb=v=ebpb−𝟏.F(\theta)^{-1}s_{b}=v=\frac{e_{b}}{p_{b}}-\mathbf{1}.

Finally, using (sa=ea−p)(s_{a}=e_{a}-p), we have sa⊤​F​(θ)−1​sb=sa⊤​(ebpb−𝟏)s_{a}^{\top}F(\theta)^{-1}s_{b}=s_{a}^{\top}\left(\frac{e_{b}}{p_{b}}-\mathbf{1}\right). Since sa⊤​𝟏=0s_{a}^{\top}\mathbf{1}=0, this simplifies to

sa⊤​F​(θ)−1​sb=sa⊤​ebpb=𝟏{a=b}−pbpb=𝟏{a=b}pb−1.s_{a}^{\top}F(\theta)^{-1}s_{b}=\frac{s_{a}^{\top}e_{b}}{p_{b}}=\frac{\mathbf{1}\{a=b\}-p_{b}}{p_{b}}=\frac{\mathbf{1}\{a=b\}}{p_{b}}-1.

Moreover, multiplying both sides by (pa)(p_{a}) gives the equivalent form

pasa⊤F(θ)−1sb=𝟏{a=b}−pa.p_{a}\,s_{a}^{\top}F(\theta)^{-1}s_{b}=\mathbf{1}\{a=b\}-p_{a}.

∎

Lemma 2 (Trajectory score-function identity).

Let τ∼pθ​(τ)\tau\sim p_{\theta}(\tau) be a differentiable trajectory distribution, and let f⁡(τ,θ)f(\tau,\theta) be any differentiable function. Then

∇θ𝔼τ∼pθ​[f⁡(τ,θ)]=𝔼τ∼pθ​[f⁡(τ,θ)​∇θ​log⁡pθ​(τ)+∇θf​(τ,θ)].\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_{\theta}}[f(\tau,\theta)]=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_{\theta}}\big[f(\tau,\theta)\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(\tau)+\nabla_{\theta}f(\tau,\theta)\big].

In particular, if ff does not depend on θ\theta, then ∇θ𝔼τ∼pθ​[f⁡(τ)]=𝔼τ∼pθ​[f⁡(τ)​∇θ​log⁡pθ​(τ)]\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_{\theta}}[f(\tau)]=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_{\theta}}\big[f(\tau)\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(\tau)\big]. Moreover,

𝔼τ∼pθ​[∇θ​log​pθ​(τ)]=0.\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_{\theta}}\big[\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(\tau)\big]=0.
Proof.

Using the definition of expectation and differentiating it gives,

∇θ𝔼τ∼pθ[f(τ,θ)]=∇θ∑τpθ(τ)f(τ,θ)=∑τ∇θpθ(τ)f(τ,θ)+∑τpθ(τ)∇θf(τ,θ).\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_{\theta}}[f(\tau,\theta)]=\nabla_{\theta}\sum_{\tau}p_{\theta}(\tau)f(\tau,\theta)=\sum_{\tau}\nabla_{\theta}p_{\theta}(\tau)\,f(\tau,\theta)+\sum_{\tau}p_{\theta}(\tau)\nabla_{\theta}f(\tau,\theta).

Next, we use ∇θpθ​(τ)=pθ​(τ)​∇θ​log⁡pθ​(τ)\nabla_{\theta}p_{\theta}(\tau)=p_{\theta}(\tau)\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(\tau), to get

∇θ𝔼τ∼pθ​[f⁡(τ,θ)]\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_{\theta}}[f(\tau,\theta)] =∑τpθ​(τ)​f​(τ,θ)​∇θ​log⁡pθ​(τ)+∑τpθ​(τ)​∇θf​(τ,θ)\displaystyle=\sum_{\tau}p_{\theta}(\tau)f(\tau,\theta)\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(\tau)+\sum_{\tau}p_{\theta}(\tau)\nabla_{\theta}f(\tau,\theta)
=𝔼τ∼pθ​[f⁡(τ,θ)​∇θ​log⁡pθ​(τ)+∇θf​(τ,θ)],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_{\theta}}\big[f(\tau,\theta)\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(\tau)+\nabla_{\theta}f(\tau,\theta)\big],

Now, if ff does not depend on θ\theta, the second term vanishes. Finally,

𝔼τ∼pθ[∇θlogpθ(τ)]=∑τpθ(τ)∇θlogpθ(τ)=∑τ∇θpθ(τ)=∇θ∑τpθ(τ)=∇θ1=0.\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim p_{\theta}}\big[\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(\tau)\big]=\sum_{\tau}p_{\theta}(\tau)\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(\tau)=\sum_{\tau}\nabla_{\theta}p_{\theta}(\tau)=\nabla_{\theta}\sum_{\tau}p_{\theta}(\tau)=\nabla_{\theta}1=0.

∎

Lemma 3.

Let Φ:Π→ℝ\Phi:\Pi\to\mathbb{R} be a differentiable strictly convex function, and let

DΦ(π∥ρ):=Φ(π)−Φ(ρ)−⟨∇Φ(ρ),π−ρ⟩D_{\Phi}(\pi\|\rho):=\Phi(\pi)-\Phi(\rho)-\langle\nabla\Phi(\rho),\,\pi-\rho\rangle

denote the Bregman divergence induced by Φ\Phi. For the following mirror-descent trust-region update:

πi+1∈argminπ∈Π{⟨∇ℓi(πi),π⟩+1ηDΦ(π∥πi)},\pi^{i+1}\in\arg\min_{\pi\in\Pi}\left\{\langle\nabla\ell_{i}(\pi^{i}),\pi\rangle+\frac{1}{\eta}D_{\Phi}(\pi\|\pi^{i})\right\},

we have, for all π∈Π\pi\in\Pi,

⟨η∇ℓi(πi)+∇Φ(πi+1)−∇Φ(πi),π−πi+1⟩≥0.\big\langle\eta\nabla\ell_{i}(\pi^{i})+\nabla\Phi(\pi^{i+1})-\nabla\Phi(\pi^{i}),\,\pi-\pi^{i+1}\big\rangle\geq 0.
Proof.

The objective is convex in π\pi, and πi+1\pi^{i+1} is a minimizer over the convex set Π\Pi. Therefore, the standard first-order optimality condition gives

⟨∇ℓi​(πi)+1η​(∇Φ​(πi+1)−∇Φ​(πi)),π−πi+1⟩≥0,\big\langle\nabla\ell_{i}(\pi^{i})+\frac{1}{\eta}\big(\nabla\Phi(\pi^{i+1})-\nabla\Phi(\pi^{i})\big),\,\pi-\pi^{i+1}\big\rangle\geq 0,

for all π∈Π\pi\in\Pi. Multiplying by η\eta gives the final inequality. ∎

Lemma 4.

For any differentiable strictly convex Φ\Phi and any u,v,wu,v,w in its domain,

⟨∇Φ​(u)−∇Φ​(v),w−u⟩=DΦ​(w,v)−DΦ​(w,u)−DΦ​(u,v).\big\langle\nabla\Phi(u)-\nabla\Phi(v),\,w-u\big\rangle=D_{\Phi}(w,v)-D_{\Phi}(w,u)-D_{\Phi}(u,v).
Proof.

By definition,

DΦ​(x,y)=Φ⁡(x)−Φ⁡(y)−⟨∇Φ​(y),x−y⟩.D_{\Phi}(x,y)=\Phi(x)-\Phi(y)-\langle\nabla\Phi(y),x-y\rangle.

Upon expanding DΦ​(w,v)−DΦ​(w,u)−DΦ​(u,v)D_{\Phi}(w,v)-D_{\Phi}(w,u)-D_{\Phi}(u,v) and rearranging terms gives

Φ⁡(w)−Φ⁡(v)−⟨∇Φ​(v),w−v⟩−Φ⁡(w)+Φ⁡(u)+⟨∇Φ​(u),w−u⟩−Φ⁡(u)+Φ⁡(v)+⟨∇Φ​(v),u−v⟩,\Phi(w)-\Phi(v)-\langle\nabla\Phi(v),w-v\rangle-\Phi(w)+\Phi(u)+\langle\nabla\Phi(u),w-u\rangle-\Phi(u)+\Phi(v)+\langle\nabla\Phi(v),u-v\rangle,

which simplifies to

⟨∇Φ​(u)−∇Φ​(v),w−u⟩.\langle\nabla\Phi(u)-\nabla\Phi(v),\,w-u\rangle.

∎

Lemma 5.

Let {ai}i≥1\{a_{i}\}_{i\geq 1} be a sequence satisfying ai+1≤(1−η)​ai+ba_{i+1}\leq(1-\eta)a_{i}+b, where η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1). Then, for all i≥1i\geq 1,

ai≤(1−η)i−1​a1+b​∑k=0i−2(1−η)k.a_{i}\leq(1-\eta)^{i-1}a_{1}+b\sum_{k=0}^{i-2}(1-\eta)^{k}.
Proof.

We prove by induction on ii. For i=1i=1, the bound reduces to a1≤a1a_{1}\leq a_{1}, which holds trivially. Next, assume the statement holds for some i≥1i\geq 1. Using the recursion and the induction hypothesis,

ai+1\displaystyle a_{i+1} ≤(1−η)​[(1−η)i−1​a1+b​∑k=0i−2(1−η)k]+b\displaystyle\leq(1-\eta)\left[(1-\eta)^{i-1}a_{1}+b\sum_{k=0}^{i-2}(1-\eta)^{k}\right]+b
=(1−η)i​a1+b​∑k=0i−2(1−η)k+1+b\displaystyle=(1-\eta)^{i}a_{1}+b\sum_{k=0}^{i-2}(1-\eta)^{k+1}+b
=(1−η)i​a1+b​∑k=0i−1(1−η)k.\displaystyle=(1-\eta)^{i}a_{1}+b\sum_{k=0}^{i-1}(1-\eta)^{k}.

This establishes the claim for i+1i+1 and completes the proof. ∎

Appendix C Experiment Details

We use 44 H200 GPUs for all our experiments. For prompts and implementation, we use SDPO’s codebase (LAS Group, ETH Zurich, 2026) on Science and Coding benchmarks whereas OPSD’s codebase (Zhao, 2026) on Mathematics benchmarks.

For DistIL, we observe performance degradation for longer sequences y∼πθ(⋅∣x)y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x), as the cumulative future loss ∑i>tH×​(⋅)\sum_{i>t}\mathrm{H}^{\times}(\cdot) grows with sequence length, leading to disproportionately large gradient magnitudes. To mitigate this effect, we apply length normalization, similar to Gu et al. (2024). Specifically, we replace the cumulative loss in future-credit assignment in Eq. (5) with

L~t+1=1T−t−1∑i>tH×(stopgrad(πθ(⋅∣x,y1:i−1,f))∥πθ(⋅∣si)).\tilde{L}_{t+1}=\frac{1}{T-t-1}\sum_{i>t}H^{\times}\big(\text{stopgrad}\big(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,y_{1:i-1},f)\big)\;\|\;\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{i})\big).

C.1 Hyperparameters for Science and Coding Benchmark

For Science and Coding benchmarks, we follow the implementation of SDPO and use their reported hyperparameters for baselines. The hyperparameters for SDPO, DistIL (Ours), and GRPO with its off-policy and on-policy variants are provided in Table 3, 4, and 5 respectively.

C.2 Hyperparameters for Maths task

For Mathematics benchmarks, we follow the implementation of OPSD and use their reported hyperparameters for baselines. The hyperparameters for SDPO, OPSD, DistIL (Ours), and GRPO are provided in Table 6 and that for SFT in Table 7. Evaluation hyperparameters are provided in Table 8 for Qwen3-4B-2507-Instruct model and Table 9 for Qwen3-8B model. The only difference between OPSD and SDPO in this scenario is that OPSD uses Forward-KL divergence whereas SDPO uses reverse-KL divergence in these mathematics experiments.

Appendix D Additional Results

D.1 More results for Coding.

SDPO evaluated their coding experiment at temperature = 0.6. We include results for that scenario in here. DistIL achieves Acc/Mean@16= 0.660\,{=}\,0.660 and Score/Mean@16= 0.482\,{=}\,0.482, outperforming SDPO (0.6430.643, 0.4670.467) and GRPO (0.6390.639, 0.4110.411). The large gap over GRPO reflects its fundamental inability to exploit execution feedback. Figure 5 notice that the same trend follows as that for temperature=0.20.2, except that GRPO becomes slightly better on Accuracy/Best@k for k=16.
